title: Gradient, intercept and uncertainty

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Reading a gradient and an intercept from a straight-line graph, and estimating the uncertainty in a reading.

blocks.heading: The gradient triangle
blocks.text: Draw a triangle whose hypotenuse lies on the line of best fit and covers at least half of it. Read the two corners on the line, not data points from the table, and write them down. Gradient = Δy/Δx, and its unit is the unit of y divided by the unit of x.

blocks.heading: The intercept
blocks.text: If the x-axis starts at zero, read the y-intercept where the line crosses the y-axis. If it does not (a false origin), calculate it: c = y − mx, using the gradient m and one point on the line.

blocks.heading: Worked example: estimating an uncertainty
blocks.text: Five timings of 20 swings of a pendulum give 28.4 s, 28.9 s, 28.6 s, 28.2 s and 28.7 s. The range is 28.9 − 28.2 = 0.7 s, so the absolute uncertainty is half of it, 0.35 s. The mean is 28.56 s. The percentage uncertainty is 0.35 ÷ 28.56 = 0.0123, which is 1.2%. Timing 20 swings rather than one keeps the uncertainty small compared with the time measured.

blocks.heading: Repeats and error
blocks.text: Repeating readings and taking the mean reduces the effect of random error, because random scatter partly cancels. It does nothing to a systematic error: a stop-watch that starts late adds the same time to every reading, however many repeats are taken.
